payload.task_text:
I manage the infrastructure team and need a full availability report for our three critical services. The raw monitoring data is in service_status_log.json in the workspace. This file contains 504 hourly status checks covering three services over seven days, from February 27 through March 5, 2026. Each entry has a timestamp, service_name, status (which is one of up, down, or degraded), response_time_ms, and error_message (null when the service is up).

Please analyze this data and create an Excel file called Service_Availability_Report.xlsx in the workspace with two sheets.

The first sheet should be called "Availability Summary" and have the following columns: Service_Name, Total_Checks, Up_Count, Down_Count, Degraded_Count, Uptime_Pct, and Avg_Response_Time_Ms. Uptime_Pct should be calculated as the number of up checks divided by total checks times 100, rounded to one decimal place. Avg_Response_Time_Ms should be rounded to two decimal places. There should be one row per service, so three rows total.

The second sheet should be called "Incidents" and list every continuous period where a service was in a down or degraded state. The columns should be Service_Name, Start_Time, End_Time, Duration_Minutes, Status, and Error_Message. A new incident row should be created each time a service transitions from up to down or degraded, and the incident ends when the service returns to up. Duration_Minutes should reflect how many minutes the incident lasted based on the timestamps.

Next, create a page in the knowledge base titled "Service Monitoring Dashboard - March 2026" that summarizes the findings. The page should describe the overall availability of each service, highlight any services with downtime or degraded performance, and note the specific incident windows.

For each service that experienced any downtime during the monitoring period, create a calendar event on the shared team calendar on March 7, 2026 from 10:00 to 10:30. Title the event "Incident Review: [Service_Name]" where you replace [Service_Name] with the actual service name. In the event description, include a brief summary of the downtime incidents for that service.

Finally, send an email from monitoring@company.com to devops-team@company.com with the subject "Service Availability Report - Week of Feb 27" that lists each service whose uptime was below 99 percent, along with their actual uptime percentage and a note about the incidents observed.

Note on existing workspace content: the knowledge base and shared calendar may contain pre-existing unrelated content such as onboarding checklists, company handbook entries, weekly all-hands, department training sessions, or Q1 budget review events. Leave those items in place. Do not delete, rename, or merge them into your incident review artifacts. Only create new pages, events, and emails for the monitoring report work described above.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, use exactly one sub-agent wave because the 504-row incident scan is the only data-heavy branch.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 1 coder sub-agent:

   1. coder 0 (office-report-builder 0): The coder sub-agent is the sole owner of `Service_Availability_Report.xlsx`. Read all 504 rows from `service_status_log.json`, sort within each of the three services, compute the exact summary metrics, and collapse each maximal consecutive down/degraded run into one incident ending at the return-to-up timestamp or observation-window boundary. Create the exact two-sheet workbook and read it back once. Return the workbook path plus a compact structured handoff containing all three summary rows and every incident row; do not create another JSON file and do not touch Notion, Calendar, or email.

After Wave 1, the main agent checks the 504-row and three-service controls once. From the returned compact handoff, it directly creates or updates exactly one page titled `Service Monitoring Dashboard - March 2026` and natively parallelizes exact event lookups/creates for services with at least one down check at 2026-03-07 10:00–10:30 using the runtime calendar default. After one page/event read-back, send exactly one email from `monitoring@company.com` to `devops-team@company.com` with subject `Service Availability Report - Week of Feb 27`, listing only services below 99 percent. Preserve unrelated objects and do not dispatch another wave.

nodes.text:
You are building an Excel availability report from raw monitoring data. Work ONLY inside the workspace: /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/SingleUserTurn-fetch-notion-monitoring/workspace

Input file: service_status_log.json (in that workspace). It contains 504 hourly status checks covering three services over seven days (2026-02-27 through 2026-03-05). Each entry has fields: timestamp, service_name, status (one of "up", "down", or "degraded"), response_time_ms, error_message (null when up).

STEP 1 - Read the data:
- Read service_status_log.json in full (use Python or filesystem reads).
- Identify all unique service names (should be exactly 3).

STEP 2 - Compute summary metrics per service:
For each service:
- Total_Checks = count of all checks for that service
- Up_Count, Down_Count, Degraded_Count
- Uptime_Pct = Up_Count / Total_Checks * 100, rounded to ONE decimal place
- Avg_Response_Time_Ms = mean of response_time_ms across ALL checks for that service (include down/degraded entries' response times), rounded to TWO decimal places

STEP 3 - Compute incidents per service:
An incident is a maximal continuous run of checks whose status is "down" or "degraded" for the same service (consecutive in chronological order by timestamp, after sorting the service's checks by timestamp ascending).
- Incident starts at the timestamp of the first non-up check in the run.
- Incident ends when the service returns to "up": End_Time = timestamp of the check where it returns to up (i.e., the first "up" check immediately following the run). If the run extends to the last check in the dataset (no return to up observed), use the timestamp of the last check in the run as End_Time.
- Duration_Minutes = (End_Time - Start_Time) in minutes, computed from the timestamps (use datetime parsing; the checks are hourly, so durations should be multiples of 60 in most cases; compute exactly).
- Status column = the status value for the incident: if the run's checks are all "down" use "down"; all "degraded" use "degraded"; if mixed, use "down" (the more severe) — but only if the checks are truly mixed in a single run. Actually, record the status of the FIRST check in the run. Wait: use this rule — record the dominant/first status: use the status of the first check of the run. Simplest correct rule: Status = status of the first check in the run.
- Error_Message = the error_message of the first check in the run (may be null; if null, put empty string or "N/A" — choose "N/A" is fine, but keep it consistent; prefer empty string if null).

Note: transitions from up -> down -> up create one incident. A service going up->degraded->down->up within consecutive non-up checks is ONE incident (first status = degraded).

STEP 4 - Create the Excel workbook:
Path: Service_Availability_Report.xlsx in the workspace.
- Use the excel MCP tools (mcp__excel__*) to create the workbook, or Python with openpyxl if excel tools fail. Prefer mcp__excel__create_workbook.
- Sheet 1 named "Availability Summary" (delete the default sheet if needed, or rename it). Columns exactly: Service_Name, Total_Checks, Up_Count, Down_Count, Degraded_Count, Uptime_Pct, Avg_Response_Time_Ms. One row per service (3 rows). Uptime_Pct values rounded to 1 decimal (e.g., 99.8), Avg_Response_Time_Ms rounded to 2 decimals.
- Sheet 2 named "Incidents". Columns exactly: Service_Name, Start_Time, End_Time, Duration_Minutes, Status, Error_Message. One row per incident. Timestamps formatted as ISO strings like "2026-02-27T14:00:00" or "2026-02-27 14:00:00" (pick one format and be consistent; ISO with 'T' is fine). Duration_Minutes as integer or number.
- After writing, READ BACK the workbook (both sheets) to verify contents match your computed values.

STEP 5 - Return a compact structured handoff in your final message:
- Workbook path: /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/SingleUserTurn-fetch-notion-monitoring/workspace/Service_Availability_Report.xlsx
- Summary rows as a JSON-like list: [{"Service_Name":..., "Total_Checks":..., "Up_Count":..., "Down_Count":..., "Degraded_Count":..., "Uptime_Pct":..., "Avg_Response_Time_Ms":...}, ...]
- Incident rows as a JSON-like list: [{"Service_Name":..., "Start_Time":..., "End_Time":..., "Duration_Minutes":..., "Status":..., "Error_Message":...}, ...]
- Also report: which services have Down_Count > 0, and each service's Uptime_Pct.

Constraints:
- Do NOT create any other JSON files.
- Do NOT touch Notion, calendar, or email.
- Do NOT modify or delete any other files in the workspace.
- Verify the workbook by reading it back before finishing.

Deliverables (acceptance criteria):
1. Service_Availability_Report.xlsx exists in the workspace with exactly 2 sheets named "Availability Summary" and "Incidents" with the exact column headers listed above.
2. Summary sheet has exactly 3 data rows (one per service) with correct counts (Total_Checks should sum to 504 across services) and correct rounded percentages/averages.
3. Incidents sheet lists every maximal consecutive down/degraded run per service with correct start/end/duration.
4. Your final message includes the full compact structured handoff (all summary rows + all incident rows).
